title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.1 Python on you own computer
These notes are written from th epoint of view of working with a PC in one of LU’s computer labs. We’ll be using the Jupyter Lab environment (app). You can install essentially the same software on your own computer for free – see below.
You can install Python on your own computer. The computers in the teaching labs use the Anaconda distribution https://www.anaconda.com. It contains a lot of useful python packages and a lot more. It is free for educations use and installers are available for Windows, MacOS, and Linux. If disk space is a premium for you then search on the Anaconda site for the ‘miniconda’ version which contains the basics and there is an easy way to add any extras that you need.

title: 2  Introduction
text:
2.1.1 Python for research
The Anaconda Python distribution is NOT free for research (or commercial) use. I use the conda-forge distribution instead, this provides a very similar experience to the Anaconda distribution.
Other versions of python are available. If you do not use Anaconda/conda-forge then do make sure you are installing a one of the Python 3 variations (I advise using version 3.8 or higher). Python 2 is still available, but has some significant differences.
MacOS (and many Linux versions) come with a version of Python however these versions often lack the science libraries needed for this module and it is generally easier to install Anaconda/conda-forge.
Anaconda also comes with a range of tools for editing and running python code. Spyder is probably the best (free) choice for editing science/engineering code. You can install it separately or as part of the Anaconda installation. Another excellent choice is pyCharm.

title: 3  Welcome to your Python journey
text:
3.1 Notebooks vs code files
This is a short introduction to python and using it on University computers (and your own computer should you wish to).
This documentation is available in website form or as a single PDF. If you are viewing the website version then the links on the left will help you navigate between chapters and the links on the right allow you to navigate within a webpage.
Traditionally, python coding has been done with individual files (usually with a .py extension). These files are edited then sent to a python interpreter to execute the code. More recently, a system based on notebooks has become very popular, particularly for science/engineering applications.
In this module we will be using .ipynb format notebooks. I prefer the notebook approach for small programming tasks, but still use the .py approach for more involved work. The lab material and coursework submissions will be jupyter notebooks, but there will be examples of .py files for you to explore across the module.
crumbs: 3  Welcome to your Python journey

title: 3  Welcome to your Python journey
text:
3.1.1 Notebook quickstart
If you have not used Jupyter notebooks before then read this before going any further: Jupyter notebook quickstart
The code below is an example of python code in a Jupyter notebook - the leading notebook system for python. You can download a copy of this notebook from the Python section of the MPP001 Learn page – it is called ‘BasicNotebook.ipynb’
The code has been split into three sections–these are referred to as cells.

The first cell imports (brings in) external code libraries to extend what python can do.
The second cell sets up some parameters
The third cell does some working out and displays the results

This general format is quite common for a notebook. There are often more cells, but the general layout remains the same.
Note: in python the # symbol is used to mark what follows on the line as being a comment. This means that anything to the right of the symbol is ignored by python. This allows you to put explanatory notes in your code. It is also a quick way to turn off one or more lines of code when you are testing/debugging it.

# The code uses the stats library to generate an array of 1000 points belonging to a normal
# distribution with a mean of 20 and a standard deviation of 4

# Import required libraries
from scipy import stats
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


# Specify the properties of the normal distribution
n_sample = 1000
mean = 20
sigma = 4


# Generate an array of data belonging to the normal distribution
rand_dist1 = stats.norm.rvs(loc = mean, scale = sigma, size = n_sample)

# Check that the data meets expectations
print(f"Mean = {np.mean(rand_dist1):,.4f} and stddev = {np.std(rand_dist1):,.4f}")
print(stats.normaltest(rand_dist1))

# Plot the histogram of the data and the distribution function
count, bins, ignored = plt.hist(rand_dist1, 50, density=True)

plt.plot(bins, 1/(sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)) * np.exp( - (bins - mean)**2 / (2 * sigma**2)), linewidth=2, color='r')
plt.show()

Mean = 20.3478 and stddev = 3.9695
NormaltestResult(statistic=2.74838621513032, pvalue=0.2530436924927925)

3.2 Text blocks in notebooks
You can also have blocks of text in notebooks. These allow various formatting options:

Bold
Itallic
highlighted

And maths is quite easy for example $ E = mc^2$ generates: $ E = mc^2$ - this is ‘in-line’ maths. Pairs of dollar symbols will generate centred maths on its own line e.g. $$ E = mc^2$$ gives \[ E = mc^2\]
For text blocks Jupyter Notebooks use a formatting system called Markdown – it can do a lot more than shown above. Have a look here for more details: https://www.markdownguide.org/basic-syntax/ (or here Jupyter markdown docs)

6.3 Starting Jupyter
On a University PC: In the search box type Anaconda. Amongst the options you should see ‘Anaconda Navigator’ - select this.
Once Anaconda has started: Click on ‘Launch’ in the Jupyter Lab box. This will start a browser window that looks something like this:



Screenshot of Jupyter start screen


The right hand block on this screen allows you to create and start editing files of different types. The left hand block determines where those files will end up.






Important



on startup Jupyter defaults to the main user folder on the PC - you must not save your files here - they are wiped at 6am every day. Instead click on OneDrive-Loughborough University to take you to your OneDrive space. I advise creating a folder there for your MPP001 work.


Once in your MPP001 folder you can click on the ‘Python 3’ square just below Notebook in the righthand block. This will start a new notebook:  Click in the light-grey box to begin to write code. An easy starter is:
print('Hello world!')`
Press Shift and Return at the same time to execute the code in the block. You should get something like this:



Screenshot of notebook with ‘Hello world!’ code


Notice that the box you typed in now has a number - this tells you that the code in it has been executed and when there is more than one code block it lets you work out the order of running the blocks. Second the text ‘Hello world!’ has appeared below the block – this is the output of the python code. Finally, a new empty block awaits your input.
If you had just pressed return then you would have gone to a new line in the block and you could have added more code.
You can go back to a cell to modify it and/or re-run it. To do this, just click in the cell.
Blocks in notebooks can be one of 3 kinds: Code - the default, Markdown – useful for text, images, etc., and Raw - we are unlikely to use this. You can change a block type by clicking on the word Code in the top-bar of the window.
You can find out more about notebooks at this link
The code below is an example of a small Jupyter notebook. The code has been split into three cells. It could have been put in a single cell, but dividing code up like this makes it easier to follow and much easier to maintain or adapt.

The first cell imports (brings in) external code libraries to extend what python itself can do.
The second cell sets up some parameters
The third cell does some working out and displays the results

This general format is quite common for a notebook. There are often more cells, but the general layout remains the same.
Note: in python the # symbol is used to mark what follows on the line as being a comment. This means that anything to the right of the symbol is ignored by python. This allows you to put explanatory notes in your code. It is also a quick way to turn off one or more lines of code when you are testing/debugging it.

# The code uses the stats library to generate an array of 1000 points belonging to a normal
# distribution with a mean of 20 and a standard deviation of 4

# Import required libraries
from scipy import stats # a suite of statistics related functions
import numpy as np # numpy provides numerical functions and storage similar to that in Matlab
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # plotting functions inspired by Matlab


# Specify the properties of the normal distribution
n_sample = 1000
mean = 20
sigma = 4


# Generate an array of data belonging to the normal distribution
rand_dist1 = stats.norm.rvs(loc = mean, scale = sigma, size = n_sample)

# Check that the data meets expectations
print(f"Mean = {np.mean(rand_dist1):.4f} and stddev = {np.std(rand_dist1):.4f}")
print(stats.normaltest(rand_dist1))

# Plot the histogram of the data and the distribution function
count, bins, ignored = plt.hist(rand_dist1, 50, density=True)

plt.plot(bins, 1/(sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)) * np.exp( - (bins - mean)**2 / (2 * sigma**2)), linewidth=2, color='r')
plt.show()

Mean = 20.05 and stddev = 3.9996

6.4 Storing values in variables
In programming we almost always need to store values e.g. in the above code the properties of the normal distribution were specified in the second block. These values are then used in the third block by referring to the variable names. The general format for assigning variables is
variable_name = value
Very often the value will be a number (e.g. lab_length = 2) however other types of information can be stored e.g.
name = 'Simon'
print(f'My name is {name}')






Note



the pair of ‘…’ around the value tell python that the value is a string (text) rather than the name of another variable. Python has a range of different variable types - you should be able to spot them as you go along. Python can usually work out the type from the context of the code.








Note



The f at the beginning of the string is important – there is more about later in this chapter.
crumbs: 6  Lab 1: Engineering Calculations with Python

title: 6  Lab 1: Engineering Calculations with Python
text:
6.5 Functions
Very often in programming we need to do use the same block of code multiple times, perhaps with different start values. One of the ways of achieving this is a function. Python has a lot of built in functions e.g. print() in the code above we’ll meet many more as the learning progresses. Most programming languages have a way of defining functions (blocks of code) for re-use so that what can be done can be extended.
In python we define a function as follows:
def function_name(parameters):
    # code block (the indenting of the code is important)

    #
    return value_returned # if any
function_name is the identifier used to reference, or ‘call’, the function. parameters is a comma separated list of one or more values that are used by the function’s code block. The code block can produce output as it runs or return a value to the point in the code that it was called.

title: 6  Lab 1: Engineering Calculations with Python
text:
6.6 Formatting results
In the third cell above the line
# Check that the data meets expectations
print(f"Mean = {np.mean(rand_dist1):,.4f} and stddev = {np.std(rand_dist1):,.4f}")
results in this output: Mean = 19.8415 and stddev = 3.9406
Notice that the numerical results are both given to 4 decimal places. This is no accident, the code in that print() statement is set up to control the format of the output. This process starts with the f just to the right of the first bracket. This tells Python that the string (text) that follows is likely to contain placeholders {} which can contain variables, code, and formatting information.
The first placeholder above has two parts: np.mean(rand_dist1) this calls the numpy library function mean() with rand_dist1 as its parameter value. It will return a number with a lot of decimal places. The part of the placeholder after the colon is a formatter .4f this tells Python to give the result to 4 decimal places. If you (quite sensibly) prefer to limit the number of significant figures then use g in place of the f. Try changing the formatters in the code above. You can find out more about formatters at this page. They can do more than control number precision.
The second placehold has a very similar structure. You can modify one and compare its new output to the other one to help get a feel for what the various formatters do.

title: 7  Programming (in python)
text:
7.1 Algorithms
There are two absolutely key steps in writing any computer program (this applies to any programming language):
If you can do these for the problem in hand then the process of writing the code is usually straightforward.
Put together these steps allow you to develop an algorithm for the problem you are working on. In formal computer science there is more to it than this, but we need to be pragmatic and get on with solving problems.
For MPP001 step 1 should be straightforward. As you get more ambitious with programming it can be tricky to define (and understand sufficiently well) what it is you want to do. Questions you should ask yourself include:
As you gain experience with programming you will develop you own list and learn to adjust it to the situation.
Step 2 is a vital step that has to happen before you begin to write the code. With a little practice you will be able to do this step in your head for simple problems. However, for anything involving more than a handful of lines of code it is best to write out the steps and refine them.
Of course, there are other stages – testing, optimisation/refinement, etc. but for now these are enough to get going.
crumbs: 7  Programming (in python)

title: 7  Programming (in python)
text:
Understanding what it is you want to do
Breaking this down into individual steps





What is the starting point (what information do I know)?
What result(s) should be returned/output?
What calculations etc are necessary
Are there any limits on the input/output?





7.1.1 Example: how many cans of paint?
You are tasked with working out how many cans of paint are required to coat the sides and top of a tank of diameter \(5m\) and height \(8m\) if each can covers \(2.5m^2\).
Step one: Inputs: diameter, Height, coverage per can. (limits: all should be above zero)
Outputs: Number of cans (limits: should be an integer)
Equations: the surface area of a cylinder is given by:
\[ \pi\times \textrm{diameter}\times \textrm{height}\]
and the area of an end is:
\[ \frac{\pi\times \textrm{diameter}^2}{4}\]
the number of cans will be given by:
\[N=\frac{\textrm{total surface area}}{\textrm{coverage per can}}\]
Step two A first stage-wise step through of the process could be:
1. Store input values in sensibly named variables
2. Calculate number of cans
3. Output results
This could usefully be refined to:
1. Store input values in sensibly named variables
    * Diameter = 5, Height = 8, Coverage = 2.5
2. Calculate number of cans
    * Ncans = (Surface area)/Coverage
3. Output results
    * Ncans needs to be rounded up
This is about ready to turn into python code:
# code to calculate number of cans required to paint sides and top of cylinder
import math as math # provides math functions and constants
# define values. Names should be self explanatory
Diameter = 5.0
Height = 8.0
Coverage = 2.5
NumCans = 0. # make sure that start from zero (good practice)
# Now calculate the number of cans required
# divide surface area of cylinder side + top by coverage per can
NumCans = (math.pi*Diameter*Height + math.pi*Diameter**2/4.)/Coverage
# Output Result
print(f'You require {math.ceil(NumCans)} cans of paint') # ceil rounds to the next integer
Notice the use of comments (anything after a # is a comment and does nothing code wise). These are a way to annotate the code so that it is easier to follow. It is difficult to have too many comments in your code especially if it contains more than a couple of active lines of code.
Now more complex problems will require more stages and you may go through three or four refinement stages before starting to convert to code. It is tempting to shortcut this, but you’ll be a better programmer for taking the extra time. In fact you’ll probably take less time in the end as there’ll be less wrong with your code when you write it. Also, you may find that more refinement still is needed as you start the coding – don’t worry about this it is bound to happen. As you get more practiced you will get used to making the judgement.






Important



You may feel that you want to jump into coding after Stage One and for simple problems this may work. However, it is good to get into the habit of doing both steps you will benefit in the medium term–especially if you want to evidence code development for your project and this will be expected for the main assessments on this module.

title: 8  Lab 2 The building blocks of computer code
text:
8.1 Conditional statements
In order to get a program with a useful level of complexity there are a few key building blocks. These are common to most computer languages (there will be syntax differences–for example python uses indentation of code to separate blocks whilst many others use curly brackets i.e. {}.
The building blocks key to introductory python programming are described below.
These check whether a condition is met and perform different code based on this check. The classic structure is the if statement which will execute the following code if the condition tested evaluates to TRUE. if statements can be extended in a number of ways: an else block adds code that is only run if the condition is not met. In python there is also an elif command that can be thought of as ‘else if…’
# if example
def Greater(x,y): # returns greater of x or y
    if x > y:
        return x
    elif y > x:
        return y
    else: return x # x&y must be equal, does not matter which is returned

print(Greater(4,5))


5

title: 8  Lab 2 The building blocks of computer code
text:
8.2 Loops
These are used to repeat a block of code either a fixed number of times (usually the for loop) or until some condition is met (while loop).

8.2.1 for loops
In most computer languages the for-loop increments/decrements a numeric variable through a range of values. Here is a C example
// Loop in C language - DO NOT copy to python
for (int i = 1; i < 11; ++i)
    // i goes from 1 to 10 in steps of 1
  {
    printf("%d ", i); // print current value of i
  }
Do not try and run this code in Jupyter (or any other python system) Hopefully you can see that it is designed to print out the integers from 1 to 10.
In python the loop goes through a list of values. The must all be the same type, but beyond that there are very few limits. So this example prints out the names of the primary colours:
colours = ['red','green','blue'] # a list of colours
for colour in colours: # start of the loop. The variable colour contains a different item from the list colours each time through the loop (starting with 'red')
    print(f'{colour}')
The C example above could be reproduced in python with something like:
for i in range(11): # range produces a list of integers from 0 up to the value sent in the parentheses
    print(i)
range() is a function that returns a list of numbers. It defaults to starting at 0, but this can be changed (e.g. range(1,11) would give 1, 2, …, 10).






Tip



Loops are often used for calculating sums, products, etc. make sure the variable that you are storing the result in starts from where it is supposed to. For sums (i = i+NextValue) this will usually be zero. For products (y = y*NextValue) one is a better choice.




8.2.2 while loops
While loops are another way to repeat a block of code. The loop operates as long as a condition is true. The following example produces the same output as the for loop above.
i = 0 # start value
while i < 11: # loop with condition 
    i += 1 # adds 1 to the value of i
    print(f'i = {i}')
    






TipCheck the conditions



It is easy to get the stopping conditions of a while loop wrong and if you’re lucky the loop will end sooner than you expect allowing you to see that there is a problem. However it often happens that the stop conditions are never met and the loop attempts to go on until the end of time. Forgetting to increment the loop variable is the most common mistake, but there are plenty of others - be vigilent!




8.2.3 break and continue
Python provides functions to alter a loop’s operation. These work in both for and while structures.
break stops a loop. The following loop will stop when i reaches the value 5:

for i in range(1,8): # range produces a list of integers 
    if i == 5: break
    print(i)

1

4


Quick question How would you change the loop above so that it printed out the value 5 before stopping?
continue goes to the next iteration of the loop rather than stopping the loop entirely:

i = 1 # start value
while i < 9: # loop with condition 
    i += 1 # adds 1 to the value of i
    if i == 5: continue
    print(f'i = {i}')

title: 8  Lab 2 The building blocks of computer code
text:
8.3 Functions
We’ve met these before, but for completeness here is a quick reminder
These are blocks of code that you send values to and the block returns one or more values. print() is an example of a built-in function. You can add your own functions to python code either by importing them from another file/script or by defining them in the script you are working on.
A minimal python example would be:
def HelloWorld():
    print('Hello world!')
Note the code after the def line is indented – this is how python tracks the extent of the current code block. You can see a similar use of indenting in the for loop above.
The brackets after HelloWorld can take the names of arguments (parameters) that are to be passed to the function. E.g.
def Quotient(x,y):
    print(x/y)
which could be called by Quotient(2,3). Note the order of arguments matters.
You can give arguments default values:
def Sum(x,y=3):
    return(x+y)
Calling this with Sum(4) will return 7 whereas Sum(4,2) will return 6. Note all arguments after the first with a default value must have default values.

title: 10  Lab 4: Engineering Data Analysis with Pandas
text:
10.1 Pandas
Last time out we looked at reading numerical data contained in CSV files into numpy and performing some analysis on the datasets. Numpy excels at this sort of operation. Where it struggles is mixed datasets i.e. data with columns of different types, especially non-numeric. These mixed data are often referred to as structured data. Such data are remarkably common - for a lot of work we can use Excel, but for large data sets we need a way to handle this in python.
Pandas (link: Documentation here) is an extremely widely used python library for handling/analysing structured data. For many of its operations it uses numpy but does all the preparitory work for you so that your code remains readable. Other libraries for structured data are available (Polars, Dask, PySpark, etc.) in some applications these have advantages, but Pandas is the market leader and many of the alternatives essentially copy the syntax of pandas and their advantages come from how they work in the background. We are going to work with Pandas here.
Numpy is built around the array structure. Pandas is built round a data structure known as a dataframe. Users of R may have cone across this concept with that language. A dataframe is a data set that can have columns of data of different types, the columns can have titles.

10.2 Getting started
We can import pandas in the usual way. It is usually given the shortname pd.
import pandas as pd
Let’s import pandas and then import a file from last week’s lab session:

import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path
# Resolve absolute path to the dataset assuming a 'data' folder next to the notebook
data_dir = Path("data").resolve() # the path to the data folder
file_path = data_dir / "L3DataTensile.csv" # specify which file in the data folder

df = pd.read_csv(file_path)  # a dataframe called df - this is where our data is stored

Notice that there was no skipping of lines - this is possible, but in this data set we can just use the data as it comes.

Pandas can read and write (create) files of many different types - including Excel files and tables. A quick introduction to Pandas and files is here (link: Pandas: getting started with files).

10.2.1 A bit of computing terminology: methods
Python is an Object Oriented Programming (OOP) language. For this module we will generally not worry about what this means. For this module the bit we need to know is that for non-OOP languages variables are places that information is stored whereas OOP variables - often referred to as objects - have the information plus a range of built-in functionality - known as methods. In the above read_csv() and head() are methods that Pandas dataframes possess. Where ever you see something of the form: var_name.function_name() then function_name() is a method of the object var_name.

10.2.1.1 Why is this important?
The methods in pandas do a lot of work for you. One key advantage that they bring is that most methods will work on the dataframe (or defined subsection of) without having to worry about loops etc to go through each row. In fact, if you do attempt to loop through a dataframe you are likely to make your code several orders of magnitude slower. This might not matter for a few tens of data, but it rapidly becomes an issues as the size of the data increases.

title: 10  Lab 4: Engineering Data Analysis with Pandas
text:
10.7 Creating copies
Dataframes have methods for creating copies of themselves. For non OOP languages a line such as
x = y
will put a copy of whatever is stored in y in a new variable x and these variables are independent of each other. With OOP’s objects life is not so simple. The syntax above will work with Pandas objects, but there’s more going on than we might expect. Initially x will just provide a way of accessing the same memory that is used to store y - it is what is known as a shallow copy. As soon as you attempt to change the value of any part of x python/pandas will make a copy of the data and associate that copy with x only. This new copy is a deep copy. A deep copy creates a new object, this is much less confusing when you are getting started, but given that ojects can be massive (many times the size of the memory in your computer) this can cause significant performance issues. In your programming you will almost always want a deep copy and this is what pandas defaults to. Behind the scenes for things like sending objects to functions etc. python/pandas is likely to use a shallow copy. The code below shows how to make deep and shallow copies.


# use df from above

dfNew1 = df.copy()            # deep copy
dfNew2 = df         # shallow copy n.b. dfNew2 = df.copy(False) also makes a shallow copy
